content: Cystic fibrosis is a severe, life-limiting genetic disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. One of the common symptoms experienced by individuals with cystic fibrosis, particularly as the disease advances, is breathlessness or dyspnoea. The primary approach to managing breathlessness involves addressing and reversing its underlying cause. However, when this is not possible, the focus shifts to palliative care, aiming to alleviate symptoms and enhance the patient’s quality of life. Various pharmacological treatments have been employed to manage breathlessness in cystic fibrosis, delivered through different routes such as inhalation, intravenous administration, oral intake, subcutaneous injection, transmucosal methods (including buccal, sublingual, and intranasal routes), and transdermal application. Despite the range of options, there are currently no established guidelines to direct clinical practice in this area. A systematic review is therefore necessary to evaluate the efficacy and safety of these treatments. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of drugs used to relieve breathlessness in individuals with cystic fibrosis. The review aimed to determine whether these treatments improve outcomes such as quality of life, dyspnoea scores, and hospital stay duration. To identify relevant studies, the authors conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, which includes data from electronic databases and manual searches of journals and conference abstracts. The last search of this register was conducted on November 18, 2019. Additional searches for ongoing trials were performed in databases such as ClinicalTrials.gov, the ISRCTN registry, the Clinical Trials Registry India, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP), with the most recent search completed on March 6, 2020. The inclusion criteria for this review specified randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials involving individuals with cystic fibrosis who were diagnosed through a positive sweat chloride test or genetic testing and who experienced breathlessness. The studies needed to compare any drug used to alleviate breathlessness with another drug, regardless of the route of administration. The authors evaluated the search results based on these predefined criteria. However, the updated searches in 2020 identified two ongoing studies that were not relevant to the review question. Previous searches had identified only one study, which was a cross-over trial. Unfortunately, this study did not meet the inclusion criteria because it did not provide data from the first treatment period alone. In conclusion, the review found no evidence to inform clinical practice regarding the use of drugs to manage breathlessness in cystic fibrosis. The authors emphasize the urgent need for targeted research in this area, taking into account ethical considerations. Future studies should focus on evaluating the efficacy and safety of these treatments, with outcomes measured in terms of improvements in quality of life, dyspnoea scores, and hospital stay duration.
